summary:
Pahang stands under the national framework of Malaysia. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 criminalise "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and acts of gross indecency, carrying up to 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping. These provisions are not limited by gender or consent and apply to visitors as well as citizens.

Every state and the federal territories maintain Sharia enactments that criminalise cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim foreign visitor is not exposed to them, while the Penal Code reaches everyone.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded in Malaysia, and no federal law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. A dual court system applies Sharia jurisdiction to Muslims only.

Enforcement against LGBT people is documented across the federation and has continued since the 2018 election. An October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur produced at least 20 arrests; an August raid on an LGBT venue detained twenty men; a Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned; and in November 2023 the state of Johor announced plans for conversion-therapy centres. The documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops, and tourists are rarely targeted for private consensual conduct.

Human Rights Watch interviewed 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021. Pahang is among the states where interviewees lived, but the report records national-level patterns and no Pahang-specific enforcement case. Government-run "rehabilitation" programmes had drawn at least 1,733 attendees as of June 2021.

Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported, and transgender people are particularly vulnerable to both.
tangentialFactors:
The Human Rights Watch study underlying these findings is titled "I Don't Want to Change Myself — Anti-LGBT Conversion Practices, Discrimination, and Violence in Malaysia" and was published on 10 August 2022 with Justice for Sisters; it treats conversion practices as a nationwide phenomenon rather than a regional one.

State-level religious enforcement varies in severity: caning as a sentence for same-sex conduct has been ordered by a Sharia court in Terengganu, while conversion-therapy provision was proposed in Johor. Pahang sits within the same statutory layer without documented cases of its own.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile was last updated on 16 December 2025, so its account of the Penal Code and Sharia provisions reflects the position at that date.
localsOnly:
Malaysians who are Muslim face both the federal Penal Code and their state Sharia enactment, which reaches cross-dressing and same-sex intimacy; enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments and the laws contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

No legal gender-recognition procedure exists, so residents cannot obtain documents matching their gender identity, and no federal anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity.

Government-run "rehabilitation" programmes had drawn at least 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and a dual court system routes Muslim defendants to Sharia jurisdiction.

Residents of Pahang were among those interviewed for the 2022 Human Rights Watch study, which documents harassment of LGBT activists and organisations and raids on private events at national level.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Pahang-specific enforcement case appears in the sources reviewed; whether the state has prosecuted or raided on these grounds in the period covered is unresolved and not sourced here.

The exact wording and penalty range of Pahang's own Sharia cross-dressing enactment are not sourced in this inventory; the figures cited (three years, RM5,000, six strokes) are the national range reported for such enactments.

Whether Pahang operates conversion or "rehabilitation" programmes of the kind announced in Johor is not sourced.

Recent Pahang-specific arrest, caning or prosecution figures are not sourced; the enforcement examples date from 2022 to 2023 and come from other states.
